Ltd; advance payment guarantee bond (No. 1001/96) for Rs.69,508,854 issued for BAT International road rehabilitation contract; counter-indemnity guarantee (COAB/805) issued by Ceylinco; BAT International defaulted; RDA called guarantee; Peoples' Bank demanded counter-guarantee; Before: Eva Wanasundera PC, Upaly Abeyrathne J, Anil Gooneratne J; Argued 16.10.2015; Decided 11.02.2016.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Eva Wanasundera PC J: Ceylinco denied liability on counter-guarantee. Court examined documents P3-P9 (guarantee bond, extensions, correspondence) and found P3 is counter-indemnity/advance guarantee bond and must be read with related documents P4, P5, P9. High Court wrongly construed P3 in isolation and on face value without considering surrounding circumstances, factual matrix, and object/intention of parties. Court held parties knew objective was counter-indemnity sought and granted. Respondent Ceylinco attempted to hide true nature of document. Court entitled to look at surrounding circumstances and construe document to reflect parties' intentions.

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Appeal allowed; judgment of Commercial High Court dated 10.10.2002 set aside. Peoples' Bank entitled to recover Rs.69,508,854 on counter-guarantee from Ceylinco Insurance; appeal allowed with costs. Decided on 2016-02-11.

Before: Chandra Ekanayake J, Upaly Abeyrathne J, Anil Gooneratne J; Argued 18.05.2015; Decided 02.10.2015.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Anil Gooneratne J: Defendant company's Managing Director kidnapped/missing since 20.07.2006 (suspected murdered); other Director (daughter) continuously resident in Australia; wife faced death threats. Only witness Chandrasiri Perera (employee since 1996) testified company in state of collapse with no effective Board to take decisions. Evidence showed extraordinary and unavoidable situation; Court must assess reasonableness of grounds for default on subjective test (not objective); company acts through effective Board of Directors (Foss v Harbottle principle); absence of effective Board rendered it impossible to appear on summons returnable date. Balance of convenience addressed by costs award.

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Appeal allowed; order of High Court dated 20.01.2010 set aside; ex parte judgment vacated; Defendant permitted to file answer and defend action; Defendant-Petitioner-Appellant ordered to pay Rs.100,000 as costs to Plaintiff-Respondent-Respondent prior to filing answer. Decided on 2015-10-02.

Kumudini Wickremasinghe J: detailed contract law analysis; parties agreed Respondent sold bottles; Defendant admitted (letter P8 dated 6 Sept 2004) liability of Rs.17,982,358.38; Defendant's tripartite agreement claim with Malaysian supplier unsupported by contemporaneous documentation; P8 (signed two days after alleged 4 Sept 2004 meeting) is clear written acknowledgment of liability to Respondent; requires consensus ad idem and intention to create legal relations; Defendant's under-invoicing allegations with Malaysian principal collateral and irrelevant to Respondent-Defendant contract; claim in reconvention for defective/delayed goods unsupported by evidence (documents V58-V60 unprovable; witness not called).

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Appeal dismissed; High Court judgment (01.10.2009) affirmed; Respondent's claim established; Defendant liable for Rs.17,982,358.38; no evidence of discharge by payment to Malaysian supplier; claim in reconvention fails; appeal dismissed. Decided on 2025-10-07.

metadata.court: Supreme Court of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...SC (CHC) Appeal No. 38/2010; Distilleries Company of Sri Lanka v Randenigala Distilleries Lanka (Pvt) Ltd; dispute over labels/bottles used for coconut blended arrack; claims of passing off and unfair competition; Plaintiff alleges visual and phonetic similarity misleading consumers; Defendant disputes likelihood of confusion and goodwill erosion. Before: Mohan Pieris PC CJ, Chandra Ekanayake J, Rohini Marasinghe J; Argued 22.09.2014; Decided 19.12.2014.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Mohan Pieris PC CJ: comprehensive intellectual property law analysis; re judicata issue (earlier case SC CHC Appeal 38/1999) dismissed as subject matter changed (bottle/label shape different); passing off requires: (1) plaintiff's goodwill in mark; (2) defendant's misrepresentation likely to deceive; (3) damage to plaintiff's goodwill; following Reckitt & Colman v Borden (Jif Lemon case); Court held unlikely confusion when comparing get-up objectively; labels slant opposite directions, different positioning, distinct colors, Sinhala script; evidence of goodwill insufficient; damage claim unsupported (increase in defendant's sales attributable to many factors, no proof of sales diversion); unfair competition (Section 142 Intellectual Property Act) similarly fails; copying simpliciter not unfair competition; no undue advantage gain from copying shown.

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Appeal allowed; judgment of Commercial High Court (31.08.2010) set aside; Plaintiff's action dismissed with costs Rs.50,000 to Defendant. Decided on 2014-12-19.

metadata.court: Supreme Court of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...S.C (C.H.C) Appeal No. 41/2014; Richard Pieris Arpico Finance Ltd v Arpico Finance Company PLC; application for leave to appeal re interim injunction issued by High Court; Respondent (Arpico Finance) incorporated 1951, owned by Richard Pieris & Co until 1967, then purchased by Alliance Finance Ltd; Respondent established goodwill in trade names 'Arpico Finance' and 'Arpico Finance Company PLC' since 1951 without interruption (deposit base Rs.2 billion). Appellant company incorporated with name resembling Respondent's; Respondent objected to Registrar General of Companies. Before: Aluwihare PC J, Priyasath Dep PC J, Sarath de Abrew J; Argued 25, 26 June & 4 July 2014; Decided 29.09.2014.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Aluwihare PC J: interim injunction criteria under Section 54 Judicature Act requires: prima facie case, balance of convenience, equitable considerations. Plaintiff's claims: (1) infringement of trade name under Section 144 Intellectual Property Act 2003; (2) unfair competition under Section 160. Court examined case law (Ceylon Insurance Corp v United Ceylon Insurance; North Cheshire & Manchester Brewery v Manchester Brewery; Parle Products v Parle Agro); distinguished by fact 'ARPICO' is invented name (not common word like 'Insurance'); greater likelihood of confusion when invented name used by competitor in similar field. Respondent's substantial goodwill and long use (since 1951) established. Balance of convenience favors Respondent (Appellant company recent vintage, minimal deposits as of 30.04.2013). Court not satisfied Respondent failed on prima facie case, balance of convenience, or equitable grounds.

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Appeal dismissed; order of High Court (30.07.2013) granting interim injunction upheld; suspension of High Court order (02.10.2013) vacated; operation of interim injunction restored. Court directs High Court Judge to give utmost priority to final determination. No order as to costs. Decided on 2014-09-29.

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...S.C. (C.H.C.) Appeal No. 48/1999; Stassen Exports Limited v Brooke Bond Group Ltd and Brooke Bond (Ceylon) (Pvt) Ltd and Kirthisiri Jayasinghe (Patent and Trade Mark Registrar); dispute over trade mark registration No. 12307 ('Brooke Bond' mark) vs Red Medal mark (No. 53509); plaintiff seeks declaration that registration null and void and removal from register; original District Court case 1991, removed to Commercial High Court 1996. Before: Saleem Marsoof PC J, Shirani Bandaranayake J, J. de S. Balapatabandi J; Argued 22.10.2007; Written submissions 30.11.2007; Decided 15.03.2010.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Marsoof J: extensive trade mark law analysis; 19 admissions recorded; 42 issues formulated. Plaintiff challenged validity of Deed of Assignment (27.03.1981) transferring Brooke Bond mark from Brooke Bond (Ceylon) to Brooke Bond Liebig Ltd due to Power of Attorney not properly executed (only Secretary's signature when two Directors or Director+Secretary required). Court addressed question of non-user: Brooke Bond Group Ltd (registered proprietor) never engaged in trading activity in Sri Lanka; subsidiary Brooke Bond (Ceylon) Pvt Ltd blended and distributed tea. Court found High Court Judge erred in disregarding vital judicial admissions recorded at trial (Section 58 Evidence Ordinance). Plaintiff's case supported by admissions and documents A1-A4, A9-A10, A14, A29-A30, A42-A43, A50-A52 which were not objected to. High Court wrongly rejected objected documents while applying paucity of evidence standard to both parties.

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Appeal allowed; High Court judgment (22.10.1999) set aside. Case remitted for determination with consideration of admitted facts and uncontested documents. Decided on 2010-03-15.

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...SC/CHC/Appeal No: 54/2017; Kim Hyum Wook (Korean national) v Don Lalith Indralal Rajapaksha and Daisy Rajapaksha; copper export transaction dispute; plaintiff claims USD 96,000 (Rs.11,000,000) for failure to supply 15 tonnes of copper to South Korea port of Busan; agreement marked P-01 dated 03.11.2010; money received by 1st defendant's personal bank account; plaintiff met defendant through Ranasinghe introduced while in South Korea; Before: Kumudini Wickremasinghe J, Arjuna Obeyesekere J, Sampath B. Abayakoon J; Argued 09.05.2025; Written submissions 02.05.2025 & 14.07.2023; Decided 01.08.2025.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Sampath B. Abayakoon J: plaintiff (Korean national) sued to recover USD 96,000 transferred to defendant's bank account for copper supply. 1st defendant claimed P-01 fraudulent document and that company Vilasa Oseas PLC (on which agreement signed) was struck off Register 12.01.2010 (before agreement 03.11.2010). Court examined evidence: undisputed that USD 96,000 received in defendant's account; no export occurred; 1st defendant's evidence inconsistent between answer and oral testimony; P-01 (soft offer letter) and V-01 (sales agency agreement) both signed for same copper supply purpose; 1st defendant claimed no knowledge of copper export but promised commission to facilitate money transfer. High Court judge found plaintiff entitled to sue despite representing father's company; plaintiff beneficial interest in contract as disclosed principal's agent; under Jack Hunt v R.C. Wright principle.

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Appeal dismissed; High Court judgment (30.06.2017) affirmed; plaintiff recovered Rs.11,000,000 (USD 96,000); 1st defendant liable. Decided on 2025-08-01.

metadata.court: Supreme Court of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...SC CHC/APPEAL 68/2014; Anthony Surendra v Sri Lankan Airlines and Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation; copyright infringement claim over songs 'Nana nanane' and 'Rajakale Hittapu'; plaintiff seeks Rs.10 million compensation for unauthorized exploitation of songs (economic and moral rights violation); application under Section 87(3) CPC to set aside dismissal; plaintiff failed to appear for cross-examination 16.01.2012; Court dismissed action at 9.30 A.M.; plaintiff arrived 10.45 A.M. claiming traffic congestion from Narahenpita Police Station ceremonial opening. Before: Jayantha Jayasuriya PC CJ, S. Thurairaja PC J, Mahinda Samayawardhena J; Argued 30.01.2023; Written submissions 06.01.2021 & 06.02.2023; Decided 01.12.2023.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: S. Thurairaja PC J: plaintiff applied to set aside dismissal under Section 87(3) CPC (default); 2nd defendant (Sri Lanka Rupavahini) argued dismissal was under Section 145 CPC and plaintiff failed to show reasonable grounds. High Court judge allowed application, finding: (a) plaintiff interested in case; (b) plaintiff not admitted negligence; (c) plaintiff informed attorney of delay ~10.15-10.30 A.M.; (d) delay beyond plaintiff's control (extraordinary traffic); (e) no Section 145 objections raised; (f) sufficient time given (18.10.2011 to 16.01.2012). Corroborating evidence from three-wheeler driver and resident confirmed major traffic congestion 8.00-10.30 A.M. due to VIP ceremony; Kirula Road ordinary by-road; police prevented vehicle movement; no advance public notice of traffic plan.

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Appeal dismissed; High Court order granting application to set aside dismissal upheld; plaintiff permitted to continue cross-examination. Decided on 2023-12-01.

metadata.court: Supreme Court of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...S.C. (C.H.C) Appeal No. 69/2013; Shahla Cassim v Sri Lanka Savings Bank; specific performance action for agreement of sale No. 749 dated 28.06.2002; plaintiff seeks to compel execution of deed of transfer for land promised by Pramuka Savings and Development Bank Ltd at price Rs.35,000,000; plaintiff paid advance Rs.4,000,000; completion deadline 30.10.2002. Monetary Board CBSL ordered Pramuka Bank suspension 25.10.2002; business vested in Sri Lanka Savings Bank (established 2007). Plaintiff claims Sri Lanka Savings Bank successor bound by agreement. Before: P. Padman Surasena J, A.L. Shiran Gooneratne J, Arjuna Obeyesekere J; Argued 08.02.2022; Decided 22.09.2023.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: P. Padman Surasena J: examined agreement Clause 6 (specific performance/liquidated damages alternative) and Clause 5 (completion by 30.10.2002 with balance Rs.31,000,000 payment). Court analyzed three conditions for specific performance: (1) plaintiff ready/willing to pay balance; (2) owner willfully refused deed; (3) damages inadequate (issued numbered questions). Evidence: plaintiff claimed ready by selling mother's property (Deed P3) but P3 produced 'subject to proof' due to Defendant's objections. Section 68 Evidence Ordinance requires attesting witness proof for attested deeds; plaintiff called no attesting witness. Section 154A CPC provides exception if genuineness not impeached unless raised as issue. Court found Defendant impeached document's execution/genuineness (Issues 4-5); therefore formal proof required; plaintiff failed to prove readiness to complete. Agreement frustration likely due to bank suspension (impossibility of performance).

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Appeal dismissed; Commercial High Court judgment (30.05.2013) affirmed finding contract frustrated by impossibility of performance (bank suspension); Plaintiff not proven ready to complete; entitled to return of advance Rs.4,000,000 with legal interest from 01.11.2002. Decided on 2023-09-22.

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...SC/FR/135/2023; fundamental rights application by Sierra Construction Ltd (petitioner) challenging tender award decision (RDA/MFAP/ICB/OFID 2/08(a)) for Rehabilitation/Improvements B367 Piliyandala-Maharagama Road (0+000-1+800km); OFID-funded contract; 04.05.2022 bids opened; petitioner bid rejected as substantially non-responsive; award notice 02.05.2023 to 4th respondent (Maga Engineering). Petitioner claims bid substantially responsive with substantially lower price than awarded bid; petitioner seeks declaration breach Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g) Constitution. Bid prices: Maga Engineering (Pvt) Ltd LKR 1,050,691,912.98; Tudawe Bros LKR 1,192,057,671.57; International Consortium LKR 1,264,776,773.90. Before: S. Thurairaja PC J, E.A.G.R. Amarasekara J, Mahinda Samayawardhena J; Argued 15.10.2024; Written submissions 20-22.11.2024; Decided 10.02.2025.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Samayawardhena J: fundamental rights petition reviewing tender evaluation decision under Award Criteria (Clause 38.1): (a) lowest evaluated bid; (b) substantially responsive; (c) bidder qualified to perform. Section 3 Bidding Document addresses Evaluation & Qualification Criteria; Clause 2.4.2(a) requires Experience: participation as contractor/management contractor/subcontractor in at least 1 contract of road construction/rehabilitation with asphalt concrete pavement within last 5 years, value ≥ USD 2.38 Million, successfully/substantially completed, similar to proposed works. Petitioner provided 5 contracts with descriptions of similar road rehabilitation projects. Court examined whether petitioner's bid substantially responsive and whether rejection arbitrary. Technical Evaluation Committee assessment scrutinized; balance between lowest price and quality considerations per National Procurement Guidelines.

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Fundamental rights application; petitioner's bid properly evaluated; tender award to 4th respondent sustained. No breach of Articles 12(1) or 14(1)(g) found. Decided on 2025-02-10.

parties: Commanding Officer Security Forces Jaffna Division

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...S.C. (FR) No. 237/2013 (heard together with SC FR 236/2013 and 238/2013); Constance Selvaranee Niles and Thevanayaki Kunanayagam v Commander of the Army and others; fundamental rights application re illegal occupation of land in Jaffna by Sri Lanka Army; petitioner Niles purchased lot No. 2B (17 perches) by Deed of Transfer No. 810 dated 26.10.1970; petitioner Kunanayagam owned lot No. 3 (40 perches total) acquired by separate deeds; property near Jaffna Hospital adjoining Sinhala Maha Vidyalaya playground; allegedly occupied October 2012 without legal acquisition; erection of fence denying access; caretaker arranged during petitioner's absence since 2003 emigration to Australia due to war; ministerial letter 07.05.2014 directing acquisition process per Land Acquisition Act. Before: P. Padman Surasena J, Achala Wengappuli J, Mahinda Samayawardhena J; Argued 21.10.2021; Decided 27.10.2023.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Achala Wengappuli J: three consolidated applications (SC FR 236, 237, 238/2013) regarding illegal occupation of private lands in Jaffna. Court examined Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(h) Constitution (right to property and equality before law). Petitioners established paper title through registered deeds. Respondents claimed strategic military necessity post-Operation Riviresa (1996) and post-LTTE operational cessation (19.05.2009); land occupied for 512 Brigade Commander official residence. Respondents claimed acquisition process initiated per Land Acquisition Act. Petitioners denied receiving formal notice; maintained occupation illegal and uncompensated. Court reviewed Manawadu v Attorney General precedent recognizing right to own property as fundamental though not in Chapter III Constitution; requires process prescribed by law. Issue: whether illegal deprivation (without formal legal process) violates fundamental rights even when claimed for public purpose.

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Fundamental rights applications; Court findings on whether military occupation without completed legal acquisition violates Articles 12(1)/14(1)(h); relief to be determined on completion of acquisition process and compensation assessment. Decided on 2023-10-27.

metadata.court: Supreme Court of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka
parties: Commanding Officer Security Forces Jaffna Division

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...S.C. (FR) No. 238/2013 (heard with SC FR 236/2013 and 237/2013); Thevanayaki Kunanayagam v Commander of the Army and others; petitioner claims ownership lot No. 3 in Jaffna Town-West (40 perches); purchased southern half (Deed No. 801, 03.08.1969) and northern half (Deed No. 1351, 27.11.1961); alleges illegal occupation by Army in October 2012; same military objective as co-petitioners (strategic defense near hospital and school); seeking declaration of fundamental rights violation and recovery of property with vacant possession. Before: P. Padman Surasena J, Achala Wengappuli J, Mahinda Samayawardhena J; Argued 21.10.2021; Decided 27.10.2023.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Achala Wengappuli J: (same judgment as SC FR 237/2013, heard together); petitioner Kunanayagam case nearly identical factually to co-petitioner Niles; both owned adjacent Jaffna properties; both had left Sri Lanka (Kunanayagam and family moved to Australia post-1990 war damage); both maintained caretakers; both occupied by Army for same military purpose (512 Brigade residence); both denied formal notice of acquisition. Legal analysis: right to own property recognized as fundamental right (though not Chapter III); must only be denied by process prescribed by law; mere assertion of military necessity or public purpose without completed legal acquisition process insufficient; respondents' threat assessment and security justification weighed against property owners' rights and compensation obligations.

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Fundamental rights applications consolidated for SC FR 237, 238/2013 (and 236); findings on illegal occupation without lawful acquisition process; relief to depend on legal completion of acquisition and assessment of fair compensation. Decided on 2023-10-27.

metadata.court: Supreme Court of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...SC. FR. NO. 245/2019; Abdul Raheem Masaheena (female, 47 years, Islamic faith) v Attorney General, Officer-in-Charge Hasalaka Police Station, Inspector General of Police; fundamental rights application re arrest and detention for wearing yellow maxi gown with Dharmachakra (Buddhist sacred Wheel) image printed on it; incident 17.05.2019 (post-Easter Sunday bombings 21.04.2019); petitioner arrested on suspicion of wearing religious symbol; charged under Section 3 ICCPR Act and Section 291B Penal Code; detained overnight; produced Mahiyanganaya Magistrate; bail initially denied but later granted after Attorney-General advised dropping ICCPR charge (03.06.2019); criminal proceedings ultimately discontinued (12.12.2019). Before: Yasantha Kodagoda PC J, Kumudini Wickremasinghe J, A.L. Shiran Gooneratne J; Argued & Decided 30.07.2025.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Yasantha Kodagoda PC J: petitioner (female, 47, Islamic faith, housemaid background) wore maxi gown with Dharmachakra image received as gift in Kuwait; worn for ~1 year without objection; arrested 17.05.2019 in heightened post-Easter terror-bombing environment (250 killed, 500+ injured, 21.04.2019). Respondent's affidavit contained multiple conflicting narratives (informal informant report vs suspicious behavior vs crowd agitation); Notes of Investigation, Report under Section 115 CPC (B Report), and court affidavits contradictory on: how respondent learned of incident, police conduct, when crowd reacted, who made arrest. Court found 2nd Respondent's evidence unreliable due to inconsistencies and lack of corroborating evidence from traffic officer (who allegedly took photo). Dharmachakra analyzed: sacred Buddhist symbol (like Christian Cross, Hindu Om, Islamic crescent); featured in Sri Lanka national emblem; recognized symbol across Buddhist traditions; vulnerable to misinterpretation in post-terror environment with heightened communal tension.

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Fundamental rights application; petitioner's arrest violated Articles 12(1) and 13(1) Constitution (equality/arbitrary arrest); evidence insufficient and contradictory; criminal charges ultimately dropped by Attorney-General; petitioner entitled to declaration of fundamental rights violation. Relief: declaration of violation and compensation assessment (if applicable). Decided on 2025-07-30.

metadata.court: Supreme Court of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka
parties: Kamani Madhya Jinadasa (for Citizen X, HIV-positive)

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...SC. FR Application No. 434/2016; Kamani Madhya Jinadasa (Attorney-at-Law, representing Citizen X, anonymous HIV-positive person) v SriLankan Airlines Limited, Dr. Anoma Jayasinghe (Group Medical Officer), Nihal Somaweera (Secretary Ministry of Transport/Civil Aviation), Dr. Sisira Liyanage (Director National STD/AIDS Control Programme), Attorney General; employment discrimination claim; Citizen X applied to join SriLankan Airlines after Mihin Lanka Ltd closure (30.12.2016); called interview 27.09.2016; selected as cabin crew 07.10.2016 with staff identity card; medical tests ordered 19.10.2016 at Nawaloka Hospital (including HIV test); informed of test passage 26.10.2016; signed employment contract 28.10.2016. Before: Sisira J De Abrew J, Priyantha Jayawardena PC J, Nalin Perera J; Argued 08.09.2017; Decided 26.02.2018.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Sisira J De Abrew J: Citizen X knew HIV-positive status since 2013 but did not disclose on medical form; declared absence of sexually transmitted disease (10.10.2016) despite knowing HIV-positive status; airline discovered HIV-positive status during medical testing; withdrew employment offer (letter Z2) on basis of false information provided. Court examined National Policy on HIV/AIDS in World of Work Sri Lanka (June 2010): petitioner contended unnecessary to disclose HIV status in medical form; airline must have known of status before testing. Court found: (1) airline could not know Citizen X HIV-positive without his disclosure (learned in October 2016); (2) Citizen X knew status since 2013 but falsely declared absence of STD; (3) Withholding facts form constitutes breach of employee-employer trust (form explicitly warned false info could cause refusal/termination); (4) airline not at fault for requesting medical test (didn't know status beforehand); (5) petitioner failed to prove discrimination based on HIV status per se (rather, based on false information).

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Fundamental rights petition dismissed; SriLankan Airlines did not violate fundamental rights (Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g)); rejection based on false/dishonest information (breach of trust), not HIV-status discrimination per se; petitioner failed to establish airline knew/acted on HIV-positive status as reason for non-employment; no order as to costs. Decided on 2018-02-26.

metadata.court: Supreme Court of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...SC. FR. No. 56/2012; Suppiah Sivakumar v Sergeant Jayaratne, CSCs Pathirana & Abeyratne, OIC Theldeniya Police, ASP Tennakoon, IGP, Attorney General; fundamental rights application for alleged assault, arbitrary arrest, illegal detention, degrading treatment; incident 15.05.2011 ~1.30 A.M. at Bambaragala Junction during Theru celebrations and riot; petitioner (innocent citizen with wife and daughter) assaulted by 1st-3rd respondents with club for ~20 minutes despite bystander Sanjika Tharanga informing officers petitioner uninvolved and naming actual rioters; dragged 8 km to Nethulmada Kovil; publicly humiliated before relatives; brought to Theldeniya Police Station; coercively signed false statement (assaulted by private individuals, not police). Before: Buwaneka Aluwihare PC J, L.T. B Dehideniya J, Murdu N. B. Fernando PC J; Argued 30.05.2018; Decided 26.07.2018.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Aluwihare PC J: examined alleged violations of Articles 11 (right to life/dignity), 12(1) (equality), 13(1) (arbitrary arrest) Constitution. Petitioner initially arrested on complaint of riot involvement; officers claimed observed petitioner being restrained, heard he was involved; used 'minimum force.' Court found: (1) Article 13(1) not violated (chaotic midnight situation, errors in judgment understandable); (2) Article 12(1) not violated by 4th-5th respondents (investigation documents P5(a), P5(b) show proper inquiry conducted; disciplinary action taken). (3) Article 11 violated: prohibition on degrading treatment is absolute; Petitioner's documents (1R1(b)) showed no resistance/flight; assault completely unwarranted; cited Abeywickrema v Gunaratna [1997] 3 SLR 225 standard (aggravated treatment grossly humiliating individual); petitioner assaulted, detained in cell, publicly declared offender despite innocence; medical reports corroborate injuries; family witnessed humiliation.

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Fundamental rights application; Court found violation of Article 11 Constitution (degrading treatment); awarded declaration of violation. National Human Rights Commission previously found Article 11 violation and ordered Rs.5,000 compensation per respondent; recommended disciplinary action to Attorney-General. Relief: Declaration of Article 11 violation. Compensation and ongoing remedies assessed pending enforcement of HRC recommendations. Decided on 2018-07-26.

metadata.court: Supreme Court of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...SC FR Application No. 77/2018; Atham Lebbe Mohamed Nawas (Gaya Bakers proprietor) v Inspector General of Police, Officer-in-Charge Kaththankudy Police Station, Respondents; fundamental rights application (Articles 12(1), 13(1) violations); petitioner SLPP member since 2017; political harassment claim regarding false 'B' Report 17/2018; incident 07-20.01.2018; petitioner responded to friend Yohara Ummah's distress call regarding two fake CID officers demanding Rs.250,000 ransom; assisted in their arrest through '119' emergency call; subsequently charged with assaulting alleged victims; petitioner claims false report filed to prevent participation in SLPP rally (26.01.2018); Learned Magistrate Batticaloa refused arrest warrant, issued summons instead; petitioner arrested 20.01.2018 despite magistrate refusal. Before: Shiran Gooneratne J, Arjuna Obeyesekere J, K. Priyantha Fernando J; Argued 07.08.2025; Decided 17.09.2025.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Priyantha Fernando J: examined Article 12(1) (equality before law) and Article 13(1) (due process of arrest) violations. Vast inconsistencies between petitioner's version and respondents' 'B' Report. 'B' Report 17/2018 (R10): three individuals (Asath, Najath, Kaleel) assaulted by petitioner and Siraj Ahamed; dragged to secondary location (previous cannabis house); Kaleel claimed extortion motive (Asath informer); charges under Sections 314, 316, 32 Penal Code; suspects (petitioner, Kaleel, Siraj) marked absconding. Court found petitioner's claim of warrant refusal unsubstantiated (police moved only for further date, no warrant application evidenced). Regarding Article 12(1): no credible grounds for discrimination based on political opinion; fabricated story undermines claim. Regarding Article 13(1): due process followed; arrest justified by 'B' Report allegations; arrest warrantless but reasonable suspicion evidenced; CPC Schedule 1 permits warrantless arrest for Sections 314, 316 offences; reasons for arrest communicated (confirmed in police statement R9).

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Fundamental rights application dismissed; no violation of Articles 12(1) or 13(1) established. Due process followed in arrest; petitioner's factual narrative found unreliable and inconsistent with evidence; 'B' Report 17/2018 provided legal basis for arrest without warrant. Application is Dismissed. Decided on 2025-09-17.

metadata.court: Supreme Court of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...SC/FRA/79/2019; Meringnage Sugandi Dinesha Priyangani Fernando & Meringnage Mangala Pushpakumara Fernando (original petitioners) on behalf of Loku Kumarage Janidu Wathsara (minor at filing, now major); v Sub-Inspector S. Akbar (OIC Athgala Police Post), Headquarters Inspector Jayantha Gunawardane, Superintendent of Police W.G. Ginige, Inspector General of Police Pujitha Jayasundara, Government Analyst, Attorney General; fundamental rights application (Articles 12(1), 13(1) violations) concerning alleged arrest, assault, detention of minor on drugs charge; incident 02.02.2019 ~19:00 hrs at Athgala, Gampola; 17-year-old (17y 2m) allegedly dragged into three-wheeler by 1st respondent and two officers in civilian clothes without explanation; at police station ~01:00 hrs 03.02.2019, marks of severe assault observed on face; allegations: forced disclosure of drug location, fraudulent placement of heroin in pocket, forced document signing; B-Report 123/19 filed claiming 2.25g heroin recovered; petitioner remanded as normal adult (minor status not disclosed to magistrate initially); family sought children's home placement due to minor status. Before: Mahinda Samayawardhena J, Sampath B. Abayakoon J, M. Sampath K. B. Wijeratne J; Argued 06.08.2025; Decided 17.11.2025.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Abayakoon J: examined Article 13(1) (due process, reasons for arrest) and Article 12(1) (equality/non-discrimination). Original petitioners filed without legal assistance; later minor became major (age 21), requiring locus standi clarification. Conflicting versions: petitioner alleged absence of explanation, assault, fraud; 1st respondent asserted information-based raid, proper notification of charges, suspect search found heroin & others' identity card. Key findings: (1) Due process analysis (Article 13(1)): 1st respondent claimed information-led operation; suspect arrested 22:00 hrs 02.02.2019; CPC Section 17 (Children & Young Persons Ordinance 1939) inapplicable (suspect >16 yrs, classified 'Young Person,' threshold 16-18); warrant not required per Schedule 1 CPC; standard: reasonable suspicion sufficient (not prima facie proof). (2) Credibility assessment: affidavits P8 (wife), P9 (associate) filed only with counter-affidavit, not original petition (documentary integrity doubted); arrest notes show reasons communicated; Government Analyst Report dated 23.04.2019 confirmed heroin purity; suspect failed to explain identity card (uncle's, in prison) & large bank deposit receipts (Rs.83,000; Rs.50,000; Rs.560). (3) Minor procedural issue: OIC did not specify age in B-Report; however, magistrate ultimately ordered children's home placement (evidence of proper procedure downstream).

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Fundamental rights application dismissed for lack of sufficient merit. Article 13(1) not violated (reasonable suspicion, proper notification, no delay in magistrate production). Article 12(1) not violated (no discrimination established; arrest justified by credible information; Government Analyst Report confirms heroin). Dismissed without costs. Decided on 2025-11-17.

metadata.court: Supreme Court of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka
parties: Samanthi Mihindukula (Former Secretary, National Police Commission)

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...SC FR Application No. 90/2021; Thilina Rajapaksha (Executive Presenter/Producer 'Neth FM' radio station, Colombo) v Police Sergeants Ravindra Kumara, Wijebandara, Constable Jayasundera, Chief Inspector Jayatillake (Alawwa Police), Assistant Superintendent Bandara, former/current IGPs, National Police Commission former/current officers, Attorney General; fundamental rights application alleging torture, violence, illegal arrest, unlawful detention; incident 01.03.2021 ~13:00 hrs on Walakumbura, Alawwa during motorcycle traffic stop; alleged violations Articles 11 (degrading treatment), 12(1) (equality), 13(1), 13(2), 14(1)(g) Constitution; petitioner claims 1st-3rd respondents assaulted him with club/foot for ~20 minutes, attempted drug-planting threat, handcuffed detention; petitioner injured: abrasions forehead, neck, chest, lip, below eye; dental fracture (9/10 injuries per MLR); missing gold chain; hospitalized Teaching Hospital Kurunegala 03-06.03.2021. Before: P. Padman Surasena CJ, K. Priyantha Fernando J, Sampath B. Abayakoon J; Argued 26.09.2025; Decided 22.10.2025.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Priyantha Fernando J: examined Article 11 (degrading treatment - absolute, non-derogable right per Sudath Silva v. Kodituakku [1987] 2 SLR 119); Articles 12(1) (equality), and 14(1)(g) (arbitrary arrest/detention). Competing narratives: petitioner alleged unprovoked assault after refusing spot fine; respondents claimed petitioner assaulted 1st respondent after being challenged on traffic violations (negligent speed, white-line crossing), verbally abused, resisted fine; 3rd respondent arrived with additional officer; petitioner allegedly knocked head against three-wheeler. MLR findings: 10 injuries documented (8 abrasions, 1 tender, 1 grievous dental fracture); medical officer confirmed injuries consistent with petitioner's history. Court conclusions: (1) Article 11: injuries cannot be self-inflicted (particularly dental fracture requiring extensive treatment); dental injuries evidently inflicted by 1st-3rd respondents per medical corroboration; prohibition on degrading treatment absolute; violation established. (2) Article 12(1): unreasonable, arbitrary police conduct (assault without provocation, coercive document signing threats, unwarranted bag search) violates equal protection; police deviation from due legal procedures; violation established. (3) Compensation justified: Rs.25,000 each (1st-3rd respondents) = Rs.75,000 total from personal funds within two months; directed criminal investigation by Attorney General.

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Fundamental rights application allowed; Articles 11 and 12(1) violated by 1st-3rd respondents. Relief: (a) Declaration of Article 11 & 12(1) violations; (b) Rs.25,000 each respondent (1st-3rd) from personal funds = Rs.75,000 total within two months; (c) Attorney General directed to conduct criminal investigation and consider institution of criminal proceedings. Decided on 2025-10-22.

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...SC(FR) No. 222/2014; Herath Mudiyanselage Jayantha Aberathna v Chief Inspector B.W.C. Dharmaratna (OIC Teldeniya Police Station), Sub-Inspector Wijerathna, Deputy Inspector General Central Province, Inspector General of Police, Director General Civil Security Division, Attorney General; fundamental rights application alleging assault in police custody; incident 21.06.2013; petitioner Civil Security Guard attached to Teldeniya Police Station; arrested on suspicion of stealing eleven (11) pieces of sandalwood from Teldeniya Magistrate's Court premises; produced before Magistrate as suspect; bailed 24.06.2013; admitted Teldeniya Hospital with complaints of assault by 1st respondent (OIC Dharmaratna). Before: Sisira J. de Abrew J, Anil Gooneratne J, Vijith K. Malalgoda PC J; Argued & Decided 31.08.2017.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Sisira J. de Abrew J: examined Article 11 (torture/cruel/degrading treatment) violation. Petitioner alleged assault in police custody; wife's affidavit P8 (annexed only with counter-affidavit, not original petition) stated observation of assault; petitioner's face, hands, body sides swollen; medical report showed contusion on left thigh only. Court findings: (1) Documentary deficiency: supporting affidavits (P8 from wife Renuka Malkanthi Wickramasinghe, P9 from witness Charuka Iroshana Ratnayake) annexed only to counter-affidavit, not original petition; documentary integrity questioned. (2) Inconsistency: petitioner alleged assault on genital region, lower abdomen, neck, right hand; doctor observed contusion on left thigh only; petitioner did not complain of left thigh assault; discrepancy between complaint and medical findings. (3) Credibility: story deemed doubtful; burden of proof (Article 11 torture claims require 'high degree of certainty' per Channa Pieris v. Attorney General [1994] 1 SLR 1); petitioner failed to discharge burden. Application dismissed without costs.

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Fundamental rights application dismissed; petitioner failed to prove Article 11 violation with required 'high degree of certainty.' Discrepancies between narrative, witness evidence, and medical findings undermined credibility. No costs ordered. Decided on 2017-08-31.

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...S.C. (FR) No. 236/2013 (heard with 237/2013, 238/2013); Surendrani Amirthanathan v Commander of the Army, Commanding Officer Security Forces Jaffna Division, Chief Coordinator Civil Affairs Unit, Secretary Ministry of Defence, Attorney General, Divisional Secretary Jaffna, Land Commissioner General; fundamental rights application alleging illegal property seizure; petitioner resides Australia since 2003; father bought Jaffna property 1969; built dwelling; family lived until 1987 marriage; parents rented house 1988; house damaged 1990 (war); family moved Australia 2003 with caretaker arrangement; October 2012 Army illegally entered and occupied property by erecting fence, denying access; property is Lot 2A (20 perches) per Plan 665A; claimed acquisition by State per Land Acquisition Act; petitioner claims no formal acquisition process completed; seeks declaration violation Articles 12(1), 14(1)(h) Constitution (right to property, equality). Before: P. Padman Surasena J, Achala Wengappuli J, Mahinda Samayawardhena J; Argued 21 October 2021; Decided 27 October 2023.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Wengappuli J: examined fundamental right to own property (recognized by Manawadu v. Attorney General [1987] 2 SLR 30, Sharvananda CJ; although not in Chapter III Constitution, can only be denied by legal process; Article 17 UDHR & ICCPR Article 17 precedent). Three consolidated petitions (Amirthanathan - Lot 2A 20pc; Niles - Lot 2B 17pc; Kunanayagam - Lot 3 40pc); all post-war Jaffna properties; all seized October 2012 by Army; all adjacent, totaling 77 perches. Respondent's position: after Operation Riviresa (1996) & post-LTTE cessation (19.05.2009), strategic military deployments continued in Jaffna town; 20-perch parcel (with newly constructed Brigade Commander residence per RX2-RX5 photos, building plans RX8) located within larger 130+ perch area (Plan 665A); Minister Lands directive (07.05.2014) ordered acquisition process initiation per Land Acquisition Act. Critical issue: court's analysis identified multiple probabilities regarding location of occupied 20-perch land within or outside petitioners' titled lots due to petitioners' failure to provide survey demarcation of fence locations relative to lot boundaries. Probabilities: (1) fits entirely within Lot 2A (20pc); (2) within Lot 3 (40pc); (3) straddles Lot 2B (17pc); (4) spans all three lots; (5) located entirely within northern portion (Lots 1A, 1B) to which petitioners claim no title (~53 perches). Petitioners bore burden to exclude fifth probability.

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Fundamental rights petitions (SC FR 236, 237, 238/2013) dismissed without costs. Petitioners failed to establish on balance of probabilities that respondents' occupied 20-perch parcel belonged to them. Absence of survey plan or sketch demarcation precluded definitive location determination. Respondent's assertion that occupied land falls within northern lots (Lot 1A, 1B), not petitioned southern lots, rendered more probable than petitioner's claims. No violation of Articles 12(1), 14(1)(h) established. Dismissed without costs. Decided on 2023-10-27.

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...SC CHC/APPEAL 68/2014; Anthony Surendra v Sri Lankan Airlines and Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation; copyright infringement claim over songs 'Nana nanane' and 'Rajakale Hittapu'; plaintiff seeks Rs.10 million compensation for unauthorized exploitation of songs (economic and moral rights violation); application under Section 87(3) CPC to set aside dismissal; plaintiff failed to appear for cross-examination 16.01.2012; Court dismissed action at 9.30 A.M.; plaintiff arrived 10.45 A.M. claiming traffic congestion from Narahenpita Police Station ceremonial opening. Before: Jayantha Jayasuriya PC CJ, S. Thurairaja PC J, Mahinda Samayawardhena J; Argued 30.01.2023; Written submissions 06.01.2021 & 06.02.2023; Decided 01.12.2023.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: S. Thurairaja PC J: plaintiff applied to set aside dismissal under Section 87(3) CPC (default); 2nd defendant (Sri Lanka Rupavahini) argued dismissal was under Section 145 CPC and plaintiff failed to show reasonable grounds. High Court judge allowed application, finding: (a) plaintiff interested in case; (b) plaintiff not admitted negligence; (c) plaintiff informed attorney of delay ~10.15-10.30 A.M.; (d) delay beyond plaintiff's control (extraordinary traffic); (e) no Section 145 objections raised; (f) sufficient time given (18.10.2011 to 16.01.2012). Corroborating evidence from three-wheeler driver and resident confirmed major traffic congestion 8.00-10.30 A.M. due to VIP ceremony; Kirula Road ordinary by-road; police prevented vehicle movement; no advance public notice of traffic plan.

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Appeal dismissed; High Court order granting application to set aside dismissal upheld; plaintiff permitted to continue cross-examination. Decided on 2023-12-01.

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...S.C. (C.H.C) Appeal No. 69/2013; Shahla Cassim v Sri Lanka Savings Bank; specific performance action for agreement of sale No. 749 dated 28.06.2002; plaintiff seeks to compel execution of deed of transfer for land promised by Pramuka Savings and Development Bank Ltd at price Rs.35,000,000; plaintiff paid advance Rs.4,000,000; completion deadline 30.10.2002. Monetary Board CBSL ordered Pramuka Bank suspension 25.10.2002; business vested in Sri Lanka Savings Bank (established 2007). Plaintiff claims Sri Lanka Savings Bank successor bound by agreement. Before: P. Padman Surasena J, A.L. Shiran Gooneratne J, Arjuna Obeyesekere J; Argued 08.02.2022; Decided 22.09.2023.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: P. Padman Surasena J: examined agreement Clause 6 (specific performance/liquidated damages alternative) and Clause 5 (completion by 30.10.2002 with balance Rs.31,000,000 payment). Court analyzed three conditions for specific performance: (1) plaintiff ready/willing to pay balance; (2) owner willfully refused deed; (3) damages inadequate (issued numbered questions). Evidence: plaintiff claimed ready by selling mother's property (Deed P3) but P3 produced 'subject to proof' due to Defendant's objections. Section 68 Evidence Ordinance requires attesting witness proof for attested deeds; plaintiff called no attesting witness. Section 154A CPC provides exception if genuineness not impeached unless raised as issue. Court found Defendant impeached document's execution/genuineness (Issues 4-5); therefore formal proof required; plaintiff failed to prove readiness to complete. Agreement frustration likely due to bank suspension (impossibility of performance).

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Appeal dismissed; Commercial High Court judgment (30.05.2013) affirmed finding contract frustrated by impossibility of performance (bank suspension); Plaintiff not proven ready to complete; entitled to return of advance Rs.4,000,000 with legal interest from 01.11.2002. Decided on 2023-09-22.

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...SC/FR/135/2023; fundamental rights application by Sierra Construction Ltd (petitioner) challenging tender award decision (RDA/MFAP/ICB/OFID 2/08(a)) for Rehabilitation/Improvements B367 Piliyandala-Maharagama Road (0+000-1+800km); OFID-funded contract; 04.05.2022 bids opened; petitioner bid rejected as substantially non-responsive; award notice 02.05.2023 to 4th respondent (Maga Engineering). Petitioner claims bid substantially responsive with substantially lower price than awarded bid; petitioner seeks declaration breach Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g) Constitution. Bid prices: Maga Engineering (Pvt) Ltd LKR 1,050,691,912.98; Tudawe Bros LKR 1,192,057,671.57; International Consortium LKR 1,264,776,773.90. Before: S. Thurairaja PC J, E.A.G.R. Amarasekara J, Mahinda Samayawardhena J; Argued 15.10.2024; Written submissions 20-22.11.2024; Decided 10.02.2025.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Samayawardhena J: fundamental rights petition reviewing tender evaluation decision under Award Criteria (Clause 38.1): (a) lowest evaluated bid; (b) substantially responsive; (c) bidder qualified to perform. Section 3 Bidding Document addresses Evaluation & Qualification Criteria; Clause 2.4.2(a) requires Experience: participation as contractor/management contractor/subcontractor in at least 1 contract of road construction/rehabilitation with asphalt concrete pavement within last 5 years, value ≥ USD 2.38 Million, successfully/substantially completed, similar to proposed works. Petitioner provided 5 contracts with descriptions of similar road rehabilitation projects. Court examined whether petitioner's bid substantially responsive and whether rejection arbitrary. Technical Evaluation Committee assessment scrutinized; balance between lowest price and quality considerations per National Procurement Guidelines.

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Fundamental rights application; petitioner's bid properly evaluated; tender award to 4th respondent sustained. No breach of Articles 12(1) or 14(1)(g) found. Decided on 2025-02-10.

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...S.C. (FR) No. 237/2013 (heard together with SC FR 236/2013 and 238/2013); Constance Selvaranee Niles and Thevanayaki Kunanayagam v Commander of the Army and others; fundamental rights application re illegal occupation of land in Jaffna by Sri Lanka Army; petitioner Niles purchased lot No. 2B (17 perches) by Deed of Transfer No. 810 dated 26.10.1970; petitioner Kunanayagam owned lot No. 3 (40 perches total) acquired by separate deeds; property near Jaffna Hospital adjoining Sinhala Maha Vidyalaya playground; allegedly occupied October 2012 without legal acquisition; erection of fence denying access; caretaker arranged during petitioner's absence since 2003 emigration to Australia due to war; ministerial letter 07.05.2014 directing acquisition process per Land Acquisition Act. Before: P. Padman Surasena J, Achala Wengappuli J, Mahinda Samayawardhena J; Argued 21.10.2021; Decided 27.10.2023.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Achala Wengappuli J: three consolidated applications (SC FR 236, 237, 238/2013) regarding illegal occupation of private lands in Jaffna. Court examined Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(h) Constitution (right to property and equality before law). Petitioners established paper title through registered deeds. Respondents claimed strategic military necessity post-Operation Riviresa (1996) and post-LTTE operational cessation (19.05.2009); land occupied for 512 Brigade Commander official residence. Respondents claimed acquisition process initiated per Land Acquisition Act. Petitioners denied receiving formal notice; maintained occupation illegal and uncompensated. Court reviewed Manawadu v Attorney General precedent recognizing right to own property as fundamental though not in Chapter III Constitution; requires process prescribed by law. Issue: whether illegal deprivation (without formal legal process) violates fundamental rights even when claimed for public purpose.

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Fundamental rights applications; Court findings on whether military occupation without completed legal acquisition violates Articles 12(1)/14(1)(h); relief to be determined on completion of acquisition process and compensation assessment. Decided on 2023-10-27.

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...S.C. (FR) No. 238/2013 (heard with SC FR 236/2013 and 237/2013); Thevanayaki Kunanayagam v Commander of the Army and others; petitioner claims ownership lot No. 3 in Jaffna Town-West (40 perches); purchased southern half (Deed No. 801, 03.08.1969) and northern half (Deed No. 1351, 27.11.1961); alleges illegal occupation by Army in October 2012; same military objective as co-petitioners (strategic defense near hospital and school); seeking declaration of fundamental rights violation and recovery of property with vacant possession. Before: P. Padman Surasena J, Achala Wengappuli J, Mahinda Samayawardhena J; Argued 21.10.2021; Decided 27.10.2023.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Achala Wengappuli J: (same judgment as SC FR 237/2013, heard together); petitioner Kunanayagam case nearly identical factually to co-petitioner Niles; both owned adjacent Jaffna properties; both had left Sri Lanka (Kunanayagam and family moved to Australia post-1990 war damage); both maintained caretakers; both occupied by Army for same military purpose (512 Brigade residence); both denied formal notice of acquisition. Legal analysis: right to own property recognized as fundamental right (though not Chapter III); must only be denied by process prescribed by law; mere assertion of military necessity or public purpose without completed legal acquisition process insufficient; respondents' threat assessment and security justification weighed against property owners' rights and compensation obligations.

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Fundamental rights applications consolidated for SC FR 237, 238/2013 (and 236); findings on illegal occupation without lawful acquisition process; relief to depend on legal completion of acquisition and assessment of fair compensation. Decided on 2023-10-27.

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...SC. FR. NO. 245/2019; Abdul Raheem Masaheena (female, 47 years, Islamic faith) v Attorney General, Officer-in-Charge Hasalaka Police Station, Inspector General of Police; fundamental rights application re arrest and detention for wearing yellow maxi gown with Dharmachakra (Buddhist sacred Wheel) image printed on it; incident 17.05.2019 (post-Easter Sunday bombings 21.04.2019); petitioner arrested on suspicion of wearing religious symbol; charged under Section 3 ICCPR Act and Section 291B Penal Code; detained overnight; produced Mahiyanganaya Magistrate; bail initially denied but later granted after Attorney-General advised dropping ICCPR charge (03.06.2019); criminal proceedings ultimately discontinued (12.12.2019). Before: Yasantha Kodagoda PC J, Kumudini Wickremasinghe J, A.L. Shiran Gooneratne J; Argued & Decided 30.07.2025.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Yasantha Kodagoda PC J: petitioner (female, 47, Islamic faith, housemaid background) wore maxi gown with Dharmachakra image received as gift in Kuwait; worn for ~1 year without objection; arrested 17.05.2019 in heightened post-Easter terror-bombing environment (250 killed, 500+ injured, 21.04.2019). Respondent's affidavit contained multiple conflicting narratives (informal informant report vs suspicious behavior vs crowd agitation); Notes of Investigation, Report under Section 115 CPC (B Report), and court affidavits contradictory on: how respondent learned of incident, police conduct, when crowd reacted, who made arrest. Court found 2nd Respondent's evidence unreliable due to inconsistencies and lack of corroborating evidence from traffic officer (who allegedly took photo). Dharmachakra analyzed: sacred Buddhist symbol (like Christian Cross, Hindu Om, Islamic crescent); featured in Sri Lanka national emblem; recognized symbol across Buddhist traditions; vulnerable to misinterpretation in post-terror environment with heightened communal tension.

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Fundamental rights application; petitioner's arrest violated Articles 12(1) and 13(1) Constitution (equality/arbitrary arrest); evidence insufficient and contradictory; criminal charges ultimately dropped by Attorney-General; petitioner entitled to declaration of fundamental rights violation. Relief: declaration of violation and compensation assessment (if applicable). Decided on 2025-07-30.

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...SC. FR Application No. 434/2016; Kamani Madhya Jinadasa (Attorney-at-Law, representing Citizen X, anonymous HIV-positive person) v SriLankan Airlines Limited, Dr. Anoma Jayasinghe (Group Medical Officer), Nihal Somaweera (Secretary Ministry of Transport/Civil Aviation), Dr. Sisira Liyanage (Director National STD/AIDS Control Programme), Attorney General; employment discrimination claim; Citizen X applied to join SriLankan Airlines after Mihin Lanka Ltd closure (30.12.2016); called interview 27.09.2016; selected as cabin crew 07.10.2016 with staff identity card; medical tests ordered 19.10.2016 at Nawaloka Hospital (including HIV test); informed of test passage 26.10.2016; signed employment contract 28.10.2016. Before: Sisira J De Abrew J, Priyantha Jayawardena PC J, Nalin Perera J; Argued 08.09.2017; Decided 26.02.2018.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Sisira J De Abrew J: Citizen X knew HIV-positive status since 2013 but did not disclose on medical form; declared absence of sexually transmitted disease (10.10.2016) despite knowing HIV-positive status; airline discovered HIV-positive status during medical testing; withdrew employment offer (letter Z2) on basis of false information provided. Court examined National Policy on HIV/AIDS in World of Work Sri Lanka (June 2010): petitioner contended unnecessary to disclose HIV status in medical form; airline must have known of status before testing. Court found: (1) airline could not know Citizen X HIV-positive without his disclosure (learned in October 2016); (2) Citizen X knew status since 2013 but falsely declared absence of STD; (3) Withholding facts form constitutes breach of employee-employer trust (form explicitly warned false info could cause refusal/termination); (4) airline not at fault for requesting medical test (didn't know status beforehand); (5) petitioner failed to prove discrimination based on HIV status per se (rather, based on false information).

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Fundamental rights petition dismissed; SriLankan Airlines did not violate fundamental rights (Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g)); rejection based on false/dishonest information (breach of trust), not HIV-status discrimination per se; petitioner failed to establish airline knew/acted on HIV-positive status as reason for non-employment; no order as to costs. Decided on 2018-02-26.

sections.title: Header and Case Details
sections.content: IN THE SUPREME COURT...SC. FR. No. 56/2012; Suppiah Sivakumar v Sergeant Jayaratne, CSCs Pathirana & Abeyratne, OIC Theldeniya Police, ASP Tennakoon, IGP, Attorney General; fundamental rights application for alleged assault, arbitrary arrest, illegal detention, degrading treatment; incident 15.05.2011 ~1.30 A.M. at Bambaragala Junction during Theru celebrations and riot; petitioner (innocent citizen with wife and daughter) assaulted by 1st-3rd respondents with club for ~20 minutes despite bystander Sanjika Tharanga informing officers petitioner uninvolved and naming actual rioters; dragged 8 km to Nethulmada Kovil; publicly humiliated before relatives; brought to Theldeniya Police Station; coercively signed false statement (assaulted by private individuals, not police). Before: Buwaneka Aluwihare PC J, L.T. B Dehideniya J, Murdu N. B. Fernando PC J; Argued 30.05.2018; Decided 26.07.2018.

sections.title: Judgment and Legal Analysis
sections.content: Aluwihare PC J: examined alleged violations of Articles 11 (right to life/dignity), 12(1) (equality), 13(1) (arbitrary arrest) Constitution. Petitioner initially arrested on complaint of riot involvement; officers claimed observed petitioner being restrained, heard he was involved; used 'minimum force.' Court found: (1) Article 13(1) not violated (chaotic midnight situation, errors in judgment understandable); (2) Article 12(1) not violated by 4th-5th respondents (investigation documents P5(a), P5(b) show proper inquiry conducted; disciplinary action taken). (3) Article 11 violated: prohibition on degrading treatment is absolute; Petitioner's documents (1R1(b)) showed no resistance/flight; assault completely unwarranted; cited Abeywickrema v Gunaratna [1997] 3 SLR 225 standard (aggravated treatment grossly humiliating individual); petitioner assaulted, detained in cell, publicly declared offender despite innocence; medical reports corroborate injuries; family witnessed humiliation.

sections.title: Conclusion and Order
sections.content: Conclusion: Fundamental rights application; Court found violation of Article 11 Constitution (degrading treatment); awarded declaration of violation. National Human Rights Commission previously found Article 11 violation and ordered Rs.5,000 compensation per respondent; recommended disciplinary action to Attorney-General. Relief: Declaration of Article 11 violation. Compensation and ongoing remedies assessed pending enforcement of HRC recommendations. Decided on 2018-07-26.
